extracted.intended_audience: educated literary readers, theatre-goers, writers and critics (early 18th-century periodical audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidance and principles for judging and producing poetry (especially epic) and theatrical works, as offered in periodical essays; includes advice on dramatic music, character-voice, imagery, structure, and the purposes of travel for a cultivated taste. Geared to authors, critics and cultivated readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of passions
rubrics_metrics.description: A great poet shows a wonderful art in describing a variety of passions which arise in characters (e.g., Adam and Eve) upon significant events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton is praised for representing characters passing gradually through Remorse, Shame, Despair, Contrition, Prayer, and Hope to perfect and complete Repentance; the progression should feel natural and moving rather than abrupt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual progression of emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: The movement from one passion to another should be gradual and psychologically persuasive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example sequence given: triumph of guilt → remorse → shame → despair → contrition → prayer → hope → repentance; scenes should permit this unfolding (e.g., prostration, tears, penitential prayer) so the emotional arc reads as development rather than summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetical turn of sentiments / use of allegory
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetical works should give a poetical turn to their sentiments and may employ allegory to embody abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton's use of an allegory (angel with golden censer whose incense carries prayers) is commended as a poetical transformation of a scriptural image; allegory should illuminate rather than obscure the sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of scriptural/poetical images
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate scriptural or classical imagery judiciously into narration to enrich the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ezekiel's angels with many eyes, biblical altar/incense scenes—these can be worked into epic narrative to heighten solemnity and resonance when handled with taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suit parts to the actors introduced
rubrics_metrics.description: An author should fit parts, language, and incidents to the actors or characters introduced in the poem/drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton is noted for always suiting his parts to the actors whom he introduces (e.g., employing Michael appropriately in the expulsion); characters' behaviour, speech and staging should reflect their rank and nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate representation of rank and demeanour
rubrics_metrics.description: High-ranking or extraordinary characters (angels, heroes) should be described in a manner befitting their station.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Michael 'neither appears in his proper Shape, nor in that familiar manner' but as 'Man clad to meet Man' with military vest, starry helm, sword and spear—details of costume and bearing should signal rank and role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice suited to character (gender/temperament)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters' speeches must match their temperament and social/gendered sensibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eve's Complaint is praised as 'particularly soft and womanish' while Adam's speech is 'masculine and elevated'—choose diction, cadence and images appropriate to character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid redundancy and puerile detail in great scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: In describing great catastrophes or solemn events, avoid idle, redundant, or puerile imaginings that lessen the dignity of the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton is commended for avoiding Ovid's 'wanton imaginations' (e.g., wolf swimming among sheep) in the Deluge; keep imagery appropriate to the grandeur of the event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of omens and prodigies to grace the fable
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate omens and prodigies (e.g., animals pursuing prey, eclipses) can properly grace and foreshadow events in poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lion and eagle pursuing prey and the sun in eclipse are effective as omens that both embellish the narrative and prepare the reader for what follows; ensure they are judicious and meaningful, not gratuitous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast and opposition of incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast and opposition of incidents (e.g., horror vs mirth) are among the most delightful things in poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay praises shifting from melancholy prospects to scenes of mirth, love, and jollity; variety produced by contrast heightens emotional effect and keeps the reader engaged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid imaginative staging and spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe scenes with vivid, theatrical imagery so that the 'theatre of Nature' is staged to reveal particular machines or apparitions in full lustre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: darkening the heavens so a descending bright cloud of angels appears luminous; such staging directs reader attention and intensifies spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of visions and episodes to diversify limited subject
rubrics_metrics.description: When a book or passage is built on a comparatively small central circumstance, the author should extend and diversify it with surprising incidents and pleasing episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Books 11 and 12 of Paradise Lost (focused on the Removal from Paradise) are defended: though the subject is limited, Milton diversifies it with visions, episodes (Cain and Abel, hospitals, festivals, wars) so the parts are not unequal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of action (represent necessary consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: A work's action should be complete: if a fall or transgression has occurred, its necessary consequence (e.g., expulsion) must be represented to render the action whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Had Milton not represented the expulsion from Paradise, the 'Fall of Man' would not be complete and the action imperfect—completeness of sequence matters for structural integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moralizing discourse between characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogues that follow visions or events should contain noble morals and discursive reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Angel-Adam discourse is cited as 'abounding with noble Morals'; philosophical or moral reflection can deepen the poem's effect when integrated naturally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety in depicting consequences (death, disease, war, luxury)
rubrics_metrics.description: Depict the various consequences of an action in multiple registers—personal horror, public disease, war's horrors, and moral decay—so readers apprehend the scope of the event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton's placement of a hospital, visions of war, and scenes of lewdness and luxury provide a comprehensive moral anatomy of the Fall's effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatrical sound and effects must suit purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Musical devices and sound-effects in theatre should be appropriate to their dramatic purpose and genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirical description: the 'Cat-call' in British theatre 'improves the sound of nonsense' and functions like violin accompaniment; there is a 'Base Cat-call' for Tragedy and a 'Treble' for Comedy; inappropriate sounds (e.g., drums at a marriage) offend the occasion—choose sounds to match tone and decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of satirical devices to perform criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: A theatrical sound or prop can be used as an instrument to express criticism and to mark deficiencies in plays or performances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An artist uses different squeaks to denote the violation of the Unities, different sounds to show whether he aims at the Poet or the Player, and composes 'Act-tunes' for incorrigible plays; satire can be systematized as part of critical apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy should be seasoned with severity for moral recommendability
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedic entertainments are more defensible when their mirth is tempered by a degree of severity that recommends reason and authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The correspondent claims she enjoys comedies 'where the Mirth is seasoned with a certain Severity'—moral restraint in comedy can make it suitable for audiences who prize virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Travel as the last stage of education
rubrics_metrics.description: Travel should come after a solid foundation of learning; it is the final polish, not the starting point, in a youth's education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning against sending an unformed lad abroad 'to make the Tour of France and Italy' before he has fixed the first principles of manners and acquired languages; beginning with travel yields little but gawdy impressions unless prior instruction is secured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposes of travel for cultivated taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Travel should be undertaken to inspect foreign customs and policies, to unlearn national peculiarities, and to improve taste by seeing the actual places described by great authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Travel aids comparison of text to original landscape, fosters moral reflection on time's ruins, and can warm the mind to emulate ancient virtues when the traveller is 'duly temper'd and prepar'd for the Impression.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Readiness to receive impressions from places of authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: To gain aesthetic and moral benefit from seeing the scenes of great authors, the traveller must already have a prepared understanding of those authors (language and principles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seeing places without knowledge (e.g., not understanding ancient languages) is of limited use; travel augments taste only for minds equipped to compare and reflect.
